exhibits.title: Flobert Parlor Gun
exhibits.subtitle: Louis-Nicolas Flobert (Paris) and many European copyists · 1845 – c.1910

art.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 90" role="img" aria-label="Flobert parlor rifle and BB cap"><title>Flobert parlor rifle and BB cap</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="320" height="90" fill="#F3E6C8"/><path d="M40 52 L120 46 L132 50 L132 58 L120 58 L92 62 L46 72 Q36 74 38 64Z" fill="#7a4a24"/><rect x="126" y="44" width="30" height="12" rx="3" fill="#C4A354"/><rect x="154" y="47" width="120" height="5" rx="2" fill="#1C2E4A"/><path d="M138 56 q4 8 10 8" stroke="#1C2E4A" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/><circle cx="292" cy="30" r="9" fill="#C4A354"/><circle cx="292" cy="30" r="4" fill="#8c6f2c"/><text x="292" y="58" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1C2E4A" font-family="Georgia">6mm BB</text></svg>

exhibits.summary: In 1845 Flobert pressed a lead ball into a percussion cap and gave it a rim: the 6 mm Flobert "bulleted breech cap," today's .22 BB Cap. With no powder, only the primer, it was quiet and gentle enough to shoot inside a large house, and Flobert built "parlor guns" for it. The CB Cap followed around 1888.
details: Louis-Nicolas Flobert (Paris) and many European copyists
The first rimfire cartridge and the first gun built purely for indoor recreational target shooting. Every gallery rifle, and every .22 rimfire we shoot, descends from it.
Flobert-type rifles and pistols still turn up in the antique trade; NRA's Shooting Sports USA (2024) notes they can be found with caveats about condition and ammunition. No dated sale price captured.
sources: NRA Shooting Sports USA: Parlor Gun History (Art Merrill, Mar 28, 2024)

exhibits.subtitle: William Wurfflein, Philadelphia (in business 1869–1915) · 1870s – 1915

exhibits.summary: American indoor "shooting parlors" boomed again in the 1870s, giving Schuetzen-club target shooters a winter practice range. Philadelphia gunmaker William Wurfflein built parlor rifles and a new product line, mechanical gallery targets, and won a medal for his targets at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition. His 1889 catalog carried testimonials from gallery owners and trick shooters.
details: The bridge between the gentleman's parlor and the public gallery: purpose-built rifles plus mechanical, reacting iron targets sold to operators.
Wurfflein targets realized $1,200 (owl) to $4,200 (folk-art cat) at Soulis Auctions, Sept 26, 2020; a Wurfflein bullseye with drop-down bird brought $2,200 there.
sources: American Society of Arms Collectors: The Wurffleins of Philadelphia (1998, PDF)
Soulis Auctions: "World's Greatest Shooting Gallery Target Auction" (Tucker collection), prices realized, Sept 26, 2020

exhibits.title: Quackenbush Bell Target
exhibits.subtitle: H.M. Quackenbush Co., Herkimer, New York · 1880s – 1930s

art.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 90" role="img" aria-label="Quackenbush-style bullseye with bell and pop-up duck"><title>Quackenbush-style bullseye with bell and pop-up duck</title><rect width="320" height="90" fill="#F3E6C8"/><circle cx="160" cy="50" r="36" fill="#1C2E4A"/><circle cx="160" cy="50" r="26" fill="#F3E6C8"/><circle cx="160" cy="50" r="16" fill="#1C2E4A"/><circle cx="160" cy="50" r="7" fill="#C41E3A"/><path d="M226 18 q12 0 14 20 l4 6 h-36 l4 -6 q2 -20 14 -20z" fill="#C4A354"/><circle cx="226" cy="48" r="3" fill="#8c6f2c"/><g transform="translate(96 30) scale(0.8 0.8)"><ellipse cx="0" cy="0" rx="22" ry="11" fill="#C41E3A"/><circle cx="18" cy="-12" r="8" fill="#C41E3A"/><path d="M25 -13 l11 2 l-11 4z" fill="#C41E3A"/><circle cx="20" cy="-14" r="1.8" fill="#1C2E4A"/><path d="M-20 -3 l-10 -7 l3 11z" fill="#C41E3A"/><rect x="-4" y="10" width="8" height="8" fill="#1C2E4A"/></g></svg>

exhibits.summary: Henry Quackenbush, a former Remington apprentice, began making air rifles in 1876 and mass-produced "gallery guns" in the 1880s; his name appeared in shooting galleries across the country. His signature mechanical target was a heavy 12-inch concentric bullseye: hit the center and a bell rang and a painted steel duck popped up.
details: H.M. Quackenbush Co., Herkimer, New York
Proof that the "ding!" of a reacting target was a selling point from the start, and a maker who served both galleries and backyard air-rifle shooters.

The Quackenbush factory site was added to the New York State and National Registers of Historic Places in June 2023, with plans for a museum. Bell targets appear at auction regularly; no dated sold price captured.
sources: Invaluable: Quackenbush mechanical cast-iron gallery target (lot listing)

exhibits.title: Winchester Model 1890 "Gallery Gun"
exhibits.subtitle: Winchester Repeating Arms Co.; design by John & Matthew Browning · 1890 – 1932 (stock sold to 1941)

art.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 90" role="img" aria-label="Pump-action gallery rifle"><title>Pump-action gallery rifle</title><rect width="320" height="90" fill="#F3E6C8"/><path d="M8 44 L92 37 L104 42 L104 54 L92 54 L60 60 L14 72 Q6 74 6 66Z" fill="#7a4a24"/><rect x="98" y="36" width="46" height="15" rx="3" fill="#1C2E4A"/><rect x="142" y="38" width="170" height="7" rx="2" fill="#1C2E4A"/><rect x="142" y="47" width="140" height="4" rx="2" fill="#1C2E4A"/><rect x="170" y="45" width="58" height="10" rx="4" fill="#7a4a24"/><path d="M110 51 q4 10 12 10" stroke="#1C2E4A" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/><rect x="114" y="33" width="4" height="5" fill="#1C2E4A"/><text x="230" y="78" font-size="11" fill="#C41E3A" font-family="Georgia" letter-spacing="2">.22 SHORT</text></svg>

exhibits.summary: A slide-action, top-ejecting .22 with a tube magazine, chambered for one round each: .22 Short, Long, or WRF (Long Rifle only from 1919). About 849,000 were made. For years it was the standard rifle chained to the counter of American shooting galleries; the 1906 in .22 Short joined it.
details: Winchester Repeating Arms Co.; design by John & Matthew Browning
The rifle most Americans actually fired at a gallery for half a century. "Gallery gun" became its nickname.
Common enough to collect, with real gallery-used guns showing counter-tie-down wear. No dated sale captured; see the Winchester Collector forum for how to tell a genuine gallery gun.
sources: Gun Digest: Classic Firearms: Winchester Model 62 (May 2019)

exhibits.title: Winchester Model 62 Gallery
exhibits.subtitle: Winchester Repeating Arms Co. · 1932 – 1958

art.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 90" role="img" aria-label="Gallery rifle with WINCHESTER roll-mark and loading tube"><title>Gallery rifle with WINCHESTER roll-mark and loading tube</title><rect width="320" height="90" fill="#F3E6C8"/><path d="M8 44 L92 37 L104 42 L104 54 L92 54 L60 60 L14 72 Q6 74 6 66Z" fill="#7a4a24"/><rect x="98" y="34" width="52" height="18" rx="3" fill="#1C2E4A"/><text x="124" y="47" font-size="6.5" fill="#C41E3A" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial" font-weight="bold">WINCHESTER</text><rect x="148" y="38" width="164" height="7" rx="2" fill="#1C2E4A"/><rect x="148" y="47" width="134" height="4" rx="2" fill="#1C2E4A"/><path d="M250 47 l8 4 l-8 0z" fill="#C4A354"/><rect x="176" y="45" width="56" height="10" rx="4" fill="#7a4a24"/><path d="M110 52 q4 10 12 10" stroke="#1C2E4A" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/><rect x="200" y="58" width="80" height="6" rx="3" fill="#C4A354"/><text x="240" y="80" font-size="9" fill="#1C2E4A" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial">loading tube</text></svg>

exhibits.summary: The improved successor to the 1906: visible hammer, 23-inch barrel, S/L/LR interchangeable, or .22 Short only for galleries. Gallery models usually carry a big "WINCHESTER" roll-mark on the left receiver (sometimes in red) and a large triangular loading port for the operator's pre-filled 10-shot tubes.
details: The last factory gallery Winchester. Only about 3% of more than 409,000 Model 62/62As were .22 Short, which is why marked gallery guns are prized.
Gallery-marked 62As are sought by collectors (Gun Digest, 2019; Winchester Collector forum). No dated sale price captured.
sources: Gun Digest: Classic Firearms: Winchester Model 62 (May 2019)

exhibits.title: W.F. Mangels Co., Coney Island
exhibits.subtitle: William F. Mangels, "Wizard of Eighth Street," Coney Island, NY · c.1886 – 1969

art.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 90" role="img" aria-label="Light-up clown target, Mangels style"><title>Light-up clown target, Mangels style</title><rect width="320" height="90" fill="#1C2E4A"/><circle cx="160" cy="48" r="30" fill="#F3E6C8"/><path d="M130 30 L160 2 L190 30Z" fill="#C41E3A"/><circle cx="160" cy="4" r="5" fill="#C4A354"/><circle cx="148" cy="42" r="5" fill="#1C2E4A"/><circle cx="172" cy="42" r="5" fill="#C4A354"/><circle cx="160" cy="52" r="6" fill="#C41E3A"/><path d="M144 62 q16 12 32 0" stroke="#C41E3A" stroke-width="4" fill="none"/><circle cx="110" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#C4A354"/><circle cx="110" cy="45" r="3.5" fill="#C4A354"/><circle cx="110" cy="70" r="3.5" fill="#C4A354"/><circle cx="210" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#C4A354"/><circle cx="210" cy="45" r="3.5" fill="#C4A354"/><circle cx="210" cy="70" r="3.5" fill="#C4A354"/></svg>

exhibits.summary: A German immigrant machinist who by 1886 ran a Coney Island shop casting iron targets for shooting galleries, later famous for carousel mechanisms and rides like the Whip. Collectors credit Mangels with more shooting-gallery target patents than anyone, and his shop kept making targets until 1969, long after rivals quit. His Catalogue #4 sold whole mechanical galleries with steel and iron birds, ducks, boats, and clay pipes.
details: William F. Mangels, "Wizard of Eighth Street," Coney Island, NY
The defining American gallery maker, and the historian of the trade: he founded the American Museum of Public Recreation (1929) and wrote The Outdoor Amusement Industry (1952).

Top prices: the only known Mangels light-up clown "Rowdy" $32,000 and the only known Mangels crocodile $20,000 (Soulis, Sept 26, 2020). A Mangels paratrooper brought $1,020 (Morphy, Apr 2012). Whole galleries: $43,200 (Duke Farms gallery, 2009) and $60,000 (150+ targets, Elli Buk collection, May 2013), per Amusing the Zillion.
sources: Coney Island History Project: William F. Mangels (Hall of Fame)

exhibits.title: C.W. Parker, "The Amusement King"
exhibits.subtitle: C.W. Parker Amusement Co., Abilene, then Leavenworth, Kansas · 1880s – 1955

art.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 90" role="img" aria-label="Running whippet on a rocker, Parker style"><title>Running whippet on a rocker, Parker style</title><rect width="320" height="90" fill="#F3E6C8"/><path d="M90 54 q30 -24 80 -16 q30 4 44 -10 l10 4 q-6 10 -14 14 l4 26 h-8 l-6 -22 q-30 10 -70 4 l-12 18 h-8 l8 -22 q-14 -2 -28 4z" fill="#1C2E4A"/><circle cx="222" cy="28" r="2" fill="#F3E6C8"/><path d="M60 80 h200" stroke="#C41E3A" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M80 80 q60 -16 160 0" stroke="#C4A354" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/></svg>

exhibits.summary: Charles W. Parker got into show business by buying a traveling shooting gallery, then building a better one. He went on to build about 1,000 carousels and whole carnivals, but kept making galleries; a c.1910 "Catalogue of Shooting Galleries" survives. Parker targets are known for rocking, animated, and knock-down-rider mechanisms.
details: C.W. Parker Amusement Co., Abilene, then Leavenworth, Kansas
A shooting gallery was the seed of the company that, when it started, was the only carousel maker not based on the East Coast (Visit Abilene).
At Soulis (Sept 26, 2020): Parker Abilene whippet $17,000, animated owl $15,000, Indian princess $3,600, rocking target $3,000. Parker's Leavenworth carousel museum is open weekends.
sources: Visit Abilene / Dickinson County Historical Society: The Amusement King (Dec 16, 2020)

exhibits.subtitle: H.C. Evans, Emil Hoffmann, Mueller, A.J. Smith (Chicago); J.T. Dickman (Los Angeles) · c.1900 – 1930s

exhibits.summary: Chicago was the midway supply capital. H.C. Evans, Emil Hoffmann, Mueller and A.J. Smith cast targets and sold them through trade catalogs; out west, J.T. Dickman patented his "Great Clown Target with the Bright Eye" in 1911 and listed it in his 1921 Catalog E. Most targets carry no maker's mark, so catalogs and trade cards are how they are attributed.
details: H.C. Evans, Emil Hoffmann, Mueller, A.J. Smith (Chicago); J.T. Dickman (Los Angeles)
Rival foundries pushed the art: Man-in-the-Moon gongs, kicking mules, illuminated eyes, card-suit spinners.
Soulis (Sept 26, 2020): only known H.C. Evans Man in the Moon $15,000; Evans kicking mule $6,000; Dickman heart card-suit $7,500; Hoffmann illuminated-eye $2,800; owl attributed to A.J. Smith $1,300.
sources: Amusing the Zillion: Step Right Up! (Tucker, Schiffer 2014) and Mangels gallery sale

exhibits.summary: The vocabulary of the gallery: a conveyor row of knock-down ducks; owls with a bullseye belly; bell and gong targets that ring on a hit; star and card-suit spinners; rotating wheels of white clay pipes that shatter; and animated rabbits, deer and soldiers that drop, swing or light up. Mangels' catalog lists birds, ducks, boats and clay pipes in one gallery.
details: This is the direct ancestor of the Crack Shot cracker: a cheap, breakable, satisfying target that tells you instantly that you hit.

Everyday pieces are attainable: duck-form targets $300–$450, ordinary iron owls $425–$1,800, a Mangels rotating target with pipes $2,000 (Soulis, Sept 26, 2020). Many galleries were scrapped in WWI/WWII metal drives (Amusing the Zillion).

exhibits.summary: The first light-gun game. A rifle fires a beam of light; a photo-tube on a flying duck drops it when hit. Shown in 1935, advertised 1936 at $495 with 10–20 shots for a nickel. Seeburg followed with Chicken Sam (1939), Jailbird (1940), Shoot the Bear (1947) and Coon Hunt (1952).
details: Rayolite Rifle Range Co. (Tulsa) / J.P. Seeburg Corp., Chicago
It moved the gallery indoors and away from lead: same duck, same thrill, no bullet.
Collected and restored by EM-arcade hobbyists (Pinball Repair, Sands Mechanical Museum). No dated sale price captured.

exhibits.subtitle: Chicago Coin Machine Co. (Chicago Dynamic Industries) · 1961 – 1976

exhibits.summary: Coin-op "shooting galleries in a box." The 1961 Long Range Rifle Gallery used a mirror to make clown and circus targets look 15 feet away; the 1962 World's Fair Rifle Gallery used double mirrors for 20 feet. Later came black-light Super Scope (1966), Apollo Moon Shot (1969), Sharp Shooter (1971) and, fittingly, Coney Island Rifle (1976).
details: Chicago Coin Machine Co. (Chicago Dynamic Industries)
The midway gallery, miniaturized for every arcade, bowling alley and boardwalk, kept the form alive as live-fire galleries faded.
Working examples are shown at collections like the Silverball and Knapp arcades and the Torrence Collection. No dated sale price captured.

exhibits.summary: In 1968–69 Sega built electro-mechanical gun games with rear-projected moving targets and mirrored depth, starting with its own Duck Hunt (released Jan 1969). Nintendo turned failing bowling alleys into Laser Clay Shooting System ranges in 1973 and later built electro-mechanical light-gun games on the same idea.
details: Sega (Japan); Nintendo Laser Clay Shooting System (1973)
Clay pigeons, thrown targets, a light gun: the moment the gallery started to look like skeet, the same leap Crack Shot makes with crackers.
Surviving machines are rare museum and collector pieces. No dated sale price captured.

exhibits.summary: Released April 1984 in Japan and as a Vs. arcade game, then as a launch title for the NES with the Zapper light gun in October 1985. Three shots per round at ducks, plus a "Clay Shooting" mode. Over 28 million copies sold, and one infamous laughing dog.
details: Nintendo (dir. Shigeru Miyamoto; prod. Gunpei Yokoi)
The pop-culture descendant of every iron duck row. It is why "shooting gallery" still means something to people born after the galleries closed, and it is the model for our Crack Shot browser game.
Still played on original hardware, which needs a CRT TV for the Zapper to work. Nintendo trademarks belong to Nintendo; Crack Shot is not affiliated.

exhibits.summary: Disneyland opened in 1955 with a Main Street shooting gallery (to 1962), then an Adventureland Safari gallery (1962–1982), plus Frontierland's. Targets had to be repainted nightly because the shot chipped the paint. In 1985 the Frontierland Shootin' Arcade replaced its lead-pellet guns with infrared beams, as Florida had done.
details: A clear marker of the turn: America's most famous gallery kept the game but dropped the projectile.
Frontierland Shootin' Exposition still operates with infrared guns (Duchess of Disneyland, 2015; Yesterland).
sources: Duchess of Disneyland: Disneyland's original shooting galleries (Jan 9, 2015)

exhibits.summary: Iron galleries were sold for scrap in the World War metal drives or broken up so targets could be sold one by one. Live .22 galleries gave way to air guns, light guns and infrared. Lead exposure at indoor ranges became a documented public-health issue from the 1970s on, with a 1990 NRA official quoted as saying lead contamination had closed hundreds of indoor ranges in 20 years.
details: Knowing why the galleries vanished is how a revival avoids the same traps: outdoors, safe backstops, low-lead or no-lead targets, and adults only.
Intact iron galleries are "exceptionally rare" (Amusing the Zillion, 2013). We could not verify a specific law that banned live-ammo carnival galleries; treat claims of one with caution.
sources: Amusing the Zillion: Coney Island Shooting Gallery from 1940s Makes Comeback (Feb 28, 2013)
Violence Policy Center: Poisonous Pastime, sec. 1 (quotes a 1990 NRA official on lead and range closures; advocacy source)

exhibits.summary: Richard and Valerie Tucker began collecting with a row of Mangels doves in the early 1980s and wrote the only book on the subject, Step Right Up! Classic American Target and Arcade Forms (Schiffer, 2014). Their collection was sold at Soulis Auctions on Sept 26, 2020. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History holds mechanical gallery targets in its collection; San Francisco's Musée Mécanique keeps 300+ playable coin-op machines; the Coney Island History Project preserves Mangels catalogs.
details: Documentation raises value and saves pieces from the scrap pile. Crack Shot wants to add an owners' registry and photo archive to that work.
See the price notes on each maker. Prices quoted are auction results as published by the auction house; they are not appraisals.

finale.title: The Revival
finale.subtitle: Coney Island USA; backyard clubs like Crack Shot · 2013 – today
finale.summary: After Superstorm Sandy, a 1940s Mangels gallery that had stood under the Wonder Wheel was pulled out of storage at Deno's, restored, and reopened in August 2013 on Surf Avenue at Coney Island USA, believed to be the only one of its kind open to the public. Meanwhile, the Henry Garden Gun keeps a smoothbore .22 in production, and a tray of round crackers costs less than a box of clays.
details: Coney Island USA; backyard clubs like Crack Shot
The gallery never died; it just needs new shooters. That is what this club is for.
Coney Island USA gallery: in operation as of the 2013 reports. Check before you visit.
sources: Amusing the Zillion: Coney Island Shooting Gallery from 1940s Makes Comeback (Feb 28, 2013)
